slides.title: Copilot's value is real but smaller than claimed
Copilot lifted dispatcher productivity by 9 percentage points over matched accounts, though volunteers flatter the gain

claims.claim: Beta accounts scheduled far more jobs per dispatcher-hour than matched accounts
evidence: +9 pp
Change in jobs per dispatcher-hour: Beta accounts 0.11; Matched non-beta 0.02

claims.claim: They also renewed more often, but volunteers are the accounts most likely to renew anyway
evidence: +4 pp
Renewal rate: Beta accounts 0.97; Matched non-beta 0.93

claims.claim: Treat the beta gain as a ceiling until a Q1 2027 test on randomly chosen accounts confirms it
evidence: Beta: 240 volunteer accounts over 12 weeks, averaging 8.1 seats against 6.2 for all accounts and more active than the base; dispatchers also self-reported 4.1 hours saved a week
Matched non-beta accounts are Brightwork's own comparison group; the briefing pack does not say on which traits they were matched

slides.title: AI costs at most $642K of new ARR a year in Routewise deals, even if it caused the whole win-rate drop

claims.claim: The sales memo overstates what AI is worth in deals
evidence: Win rate in Routewise-contested deals: Q1–Q2 2026 0.44; Q3 2026 0.37; Implied by sales memo 0.58
Q3 2026: Routewise also cut first-year prices by 20%, so AI explains at most part of the drop
Sales memo: a third of Routewise losses is 3 times what the whole drop can explain
The memo rests on 31% of Q3 loss notes mentioning AI: a count of mentions across all lost deals, not of reasons in Routewise deals
"Implied by sales memo": the VP Sales claim that Copilot would recover a third of the deals lost to Routewise, applied to the 63% of contested deals lost in Q3 2026

claims.claim: Most new ARR a year at stake if AI caused all of the drop: $642K
evidence: 1,560 contested deals × 7 pp drop × $5,878 ARR per new account

slides.title: Why not a $149 add-on
Stated intent overstates demand: 46% of survey respondents said they were likely to buy, but only 14% paid

claims.claim: Each paying account was matched by three who only said yes
evidence: 3.2x survey intent for every account that actually paid
Said likely to buy (survey) 0.46; Paid when asked (paywall test) 0.141667
Survey: October 2026, 610 customer admins replied out of 9,800 asked. Paywall test: last four weeks of the beta, 17 of 120 beta accounts bought at $149

claims.claim: Survey: only 6% of admins replied, and their accounts average 9.4 seats, so keen, larger customers answered
evidence: 610 of 9,800 replied; 9.4 seats

claims.claim: Paywall test: a real purchase decision, but among beta volunteers who already liked the product
For the base: expect less than the paywall's 14%, not more

slides.title: At the rate accounts actually paid, the add-on brings about $2.5M of ARR, under a third of the internal case

claims.claim: the add-on brings about $2.5M of ARR
evidence: 9,800 customer accounts that could buy × 14.2% bought when asked to pay (17 of 120, paywall test) × $1,788 a year per account: $149 × 12 months = $2.5M ARR a year from the add-on, at most

claims.claim: The internal $8M case swaps paid conversion for survey intent
evidence: Same sum with the survey's 46% in place of 14% gives the CPO's $8.06M; only the conversion rate differs

claims.claim: 14% is itself an upper bound: buyers came from volunteers with 8.1 seats, against 6.2 in the base
evidence: 8.1 seats vs 6.2

slides.title: A flat $149 price draws the heaviest users, and on the top tenth it leaves almost no margin

claims.claim: The accounts that buy are the ones that cost most to serve
evidence: Inference cost per month: Median account 17.1; Mean account 32.4; Paywall buyers 61.2; Top 10% of accounts 130.5 (at $0.009 per request)
Paywall buyers: 1.9 times the mean account's requests; inference takes 41% of the price
Top 10%: inference takes 88% of the price, before platform and support cost

claims.claim: At the survey's 46%: company gross margin would fall to 74.7%, below the floor
Charge per seat with a usage allowance, so price rises with use
The pack says the top 10% sent 58% of requests, but Table 2 implies 40%; costs here use Table 2, the lower figure

slides.title: The Pro plan
Including Copilot in a Pro plan beats both the add-on and a free feature: more accounts pay and margin holds

claims.claim: $149 add-on: Fewest payers, and the heaviest users buy; Routewise does not charge extra
evidence: Accounts expected to pay 14.2%; Price $149; Copilot margin after inference 58.9%; Company gross margin stays above the 75% floor

claims.claim: Pro plan, $12 more per seat: More payers, better margin / Price rises with seats, and it matches Routewise, which bundles AI into its Pro plan
evidence: Accounts expected to pay 33%; Price per average account $74.4; Copilot margin 66.7%; Company gross margin stays above the 75% floor

claims.claim: Free inside Core: Matches Routewise but breaks the margin floor
evidence: $44.9M gross profit today ($57.6M ARR × 78%) − $2.9M inference if all 60,760 seats use Copilot at the beta average − $0.6M platform, evaluation and support ÷ $57.6M ARR unchanged = 71.9% company gross margin

claims.claim: With the add-on or Pro, company margin is 76.2% to 76.5%
evidence: Payers: 14% paywall rate for the add-on; 33% moved to the 2023 tier within a year. Inference: buyers' 6,800 requests a month (add-on); 444 per seat, the beta average (Pro)

slides.title: If a third of accounts move up as in 2023, Pro alone adds 5 percentage points of NRR, closing the gap

claims.claim: Pro alone adds 5 percentage points of NRR
evidence: 9,800 customer accounts × 33% move up within a year × $892.8 a year per account ($12 × 6.2 seats × 12) ÷ $57.6M today's ARR = 5 pp added to NRR, against a gap of 4 (101% to 105%)

claims.claim: The target holds as long as about a quarter of accounts move
evidence: Pro alone closes the gap if 26% of accounts move within a year, against 33% in 2023

claims.claim: Copilot profit with Pro is about $1.32M a year and repays the $1.47M launch cost in about 13 months, against 20 months for the add-on
evidence: after inference and the $0.6M platform cost

slides.title: A usage allowance keeps Pro profitable for heavy users and company gross margin at 76.5%, above the floor

claims.claim: Recommended design: 1,000 AI requests included per seat each month, 3.6 cents per request above the allowance
evidence: 1,000 = 2.25 times the beta average of 444
3.6 cents = 4 times the 0.9-cent contract cost
A full seat costs $9 of the $12 premium
Top-tenth seats (about 1,790) pay overage
Earns 75% margin on each extra request

claims.claim: 76.5% company gross margin with Pro
evidence: Floor 75%; today 78%
$44.9M gross profit today + $2.9M Pro ARR − $0.96M inference for Pro accounts − $0.6M platform and support = 76.5% of revenue with Pro
Free in Core: 71.9%

claims.claim: Review when the contract ends
evidence: List prices fell 35% in a year

slides.title: The trade-off with mobile
Mobile reliability, not AI, is what customers leave over and ask for first

claims.claim: Mobile drives 4.5 times as much churn as AI features
evidence: Main reason for leaving (n = 1,190): Mobile app reliability 0.27; Price 0.22; Missing integrations 0.15; Out of business or sold 0.14; Switched for AI features 0.06; Other 0.16

claims.claim: A reliable mobile app is also the top request, twice as often as AI scheduling
evidence: 2x
Ranked first: Reliable technician mobile app 0.38; AI scheduling 0.19

claims.claim: Churn citing mobile costs about $2.18M of ARR a year, against $0.48M for AI features
evidence: ARR lost estimated as share of churn × 14% annual logo churn × $57.6M ARR, assuming churned accounts are average size

slides.title: Copilot first is the better sequence unless the mobile rewrite would remove more than about half of mobile-driven churn

claims.claim: Copilot first: launch Q2 2027 — Ahead through 2028 / Pro revenue also arrives two quarters sooner, and the mobile loss assumes the rewrite fixes all of it
evidence: Mobile rewrite waits: churn citing mobile runs two more quarters; ARR lost for good, at most $1,089K

claims.claim: Mobile first: Copilot in Q4 2027 — Better only if the rewrite fixes most mobile churn
evidence: Copilot waits: Routewise deal losses and AI-driven churn run on; ARR lost for good, at most $563K

claims.claim: Break-even: 51.7% of mobile churn the rewrite must remove to justify going first
evidence: $563K lost if Copilot waits (half a year of $642K in deals and $484K in AI churn) ÷ $1,089K lost if mobile waits (half a year of $2.18M in mobile churn) = 51.7%
Not counted: $1.44M of Pro revenue pushed back if Copilot waits

claims.claim: Over a longer horizon the lost mobile accounts keep costing; the case for mobile first then rests on the rewrite fixing well over half of mobile churn

slides.title: How to launch
Pro launches by mid-2027, and the mobile rewrite restarts as soon as the Copilot team frees up

claims.claim: Launch plan by workstream, Q1 2027 to Q2 2028
evidence: Copilot build (14 engineers): Harden for launch; test on random accounts; Go/no-go after test
Pro plan: Launch; Track moves to Pro against 26% in a year
Mobile rewrite: Restarts as the Copilot team frees up
Pricing and cost: Renegotiate inference; reset allowance; Contract price ends

claims.claim: The mobile rewrite takes the Copilot engineers first once the launch ships, with no new project in between
evidence: Assumes the 14 Copilot engineers work in Q1–Q2 2027, so the rewrite restarts in Q3 2027
Inference is fixed at $0.009 a request through December 2027; provider list prices fell 35% in the past year

slides.title: Four conditions keep the launch on track, and missing any one of them should reopen the decision

claims.claim: Before sign-off: CS and the mobile lead estimate how much mobile churn the rewrite would remove; above about half, put mobile first
evidence: 27% of churn cites mobile reliability (p. 15)

claims.claim: Q1 2027: run Copilot on randomly chosen non-beta accounts and launch only if jobs per dispatcher-hour beat matched accounts' gain
evidence: 2% gain of matched accounts to beat (p. 4)

claims.claim: At launch: Pro includes 1,000 requests per seat, with overage above it, so company gross margin stays above the floor
evidence: 75% company gross margin floor (p. 13)

claims.claim: First year: track moves to Pro monthly; below the run-rate for 26% in a year, add other NRR levers
evidence: 26.3% of accounts on Pro within a year (p. 12)

claims.claim: Approve the Q2 launch inside Pro at $12 more per seat, on these four conditions

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Approve the Q2 launch inside Pro at $12 more per seat, on these four conditions (a tested gain, a usage allowance, 26% Pro uptake and an early mobile restart); plan on about $2.9M of ARR, not $8M

alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: would sell to one account in seven and earn least on heavy users; 14.2% pay, about $2.5M ARR, under a third of the $8M case; fewest payers, and the heaviest users buy; Routewise does not charge extra
Chosen: earns more, keeps margin and closes the NRR gap; 33% expected to pay, 66.7% Copilot margin, company gross margin 76.5% with usage allowance
Rejected: matches Routewise but breaks the margin floor (company gross margin 71.9%, no new revenue)
Chosen: ahead through 2028; at most $1,089K lost from mobile rewrite waiting; better unless rewrite removes more than about half (51.7%) of mobile churn
Better only if the rewrite fixes most mobile churn; at most $563K lost if Copilot waits; to be checked before sign-off — above about half, put mobile first

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Synthetic benchmark data: fictional company, every number from the briefing pack
Beta accounts were volunteers who flatter the gain; treat the beta gain as a ceiling until a Q1 2027 randomized test confirms it
The briefing pack does not say on which traits matched non-beta accounts were matched
$642K assumes AI caused the whole win-rate drop; Routewise also cut first-year prices by 20%
Survey respondents (6%, 9.4 seats) skew keen and larger; paywall test was among beta volunteers; expect less than 14% for the base
14% is itself an upper bound: buyers came from volunteers with 8.1 seats, against 6.2 in the base
Add-on ARR assumes every account is offered the add-on and no buyer cancels within the year; before inference, $0.6M platform and $1.47M engineering cost
The pack says the top 10% sent 58% of requests, but Table 2 implies 40%; costs use Table 2, the lower figure
Pro NRR estimate: accounts that move average 6.2 seats; no extra churn or downgrades; any retention gain from Copilot is not counted
The 2023 tier is the only in-house benchmark; its content differed from Pro
The 1,000-request allowance and overage price are the team's recommended design, chosen in the exec team's absence; confirm at January planning
Top-tenth figure assumes those accounts have the beta average of 8.1 seats
Inference contract price $0.009 fixed through December 2027; list prices fell 35% in a year; review when the contract ends
Churn ARR assumes churned accounts are average size

Sequencing figures are upper bounds on both sides: AI caused the whole win-rate drop, Copilot stops all AI-driven churn, the rewrite stops all mobile churn; $1.44M of Pro revenue pushed back not counted
Over a longer horizon the lost mobile accounts keep costing
Assumes the 14 Copilot engineers work in Q1–Q2 2027, so the rewrite restarts in Q3 2027; its end date is not in the briefing pack
Missing any one of the four conditions should reopen the decision

normalized.extraction_notes: The deck came as plain text with no images, so there were no pictures to transcribe. Slide 18 is a Gantt-style timeline. Its bars came through as loose labels without their positions on the quarters, so I can't tell exactly which quarter each item falls in. On slides 8, 11, 12, 13 and 16, the calculation numbers and their labels were extracted separately. I paired each number with its label by the order they appear in. The governing thought is the headline line of the executive summary. The executive summary list holds the numbered points with their sub-bullets, in order.
